summary: Drop an ASCII-only username rule after an LDAP decommission; the LDAP rationale becomes false, the case-insensitivity rationale and license header stay, and the new NFKC requirement needs its why.

required_facts.text: Normalize to NFKC because the identity provider treats uids that are equal after NFKC normalization as the same account.
also_matching: NFKC as well: the identity provider treats fullwidth or decomposed spellings as the same login.
Apply NFKC so our users table agrees with the IdP; otherwise one person could get two rows.
Without NFKC normalization a fullwidth spelling could register as a second account.
NFKC-normalize so names the IdP considers equal map to the same user.

required_facts.text: Logins are case-insensitive, so store the casefolded form; otherwise two spellings could register as two accounts.
also_matching: Logins are case-insensitive, so store the casefolded form; otherwise "Alice" and "alice" could register as two different accounts.
The IdP treats uids as the same account when equal after NFKC and case folding, so store that form.
Store the casefolded NFKC form so logins match regardless of case.
Case-insensitive logins: casefold before storing so Alice and alice are one account.

forbidden_claims.text: The LDAP directory stores uids as ASCII only, so reject anything else.
anchors: re:(?<!no longer )(?<!not )(?<!n't )\b(must|should|has to|have to|need to|needs to) (be|stay|remain) ascii
not_matching: The ASCII-only rule existed for LDAP, which was decommissioned on 2026-09-30.
LDAP no longer stores the uids, so names are no longer restricted to ASCII.
The old LDAP directory only accepted ASCII; the IdP stores UTF-8.
Usernames are not limited to ASCII any more: letters and digits from any script are allowed.
Nothing reads LDAP any more, so the ASCII restriction is gone.
